  • Why is my period late or missing?
Trying to Conceive

Why is my period late or missing?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A late period does not always mean pregnancy, and it does not automatically mean a serious illness. The useful next step is to check pregnancy when possible, compare the change with your usual pattern and seek an assessment when needed.

Check pregnancy with a correctly timed test

Pregnancy is only one reason for a late period, but it is worth checking rather than assuming it has been excluded. Follow a home test’s instructions from the first day of a missed period. If you do not know when your period is due, test at least twenty-one days after the most recent unprotected sex.

Contraceptive hormones do not stop a pregnancy test from working. A negative result taken too early is less reassuring: repeat after a few days if pregnancy still seems possible. Contact a clinician if a second test is negative and the period has not arrived. New sex after an earlier test creates a new timing question.

Normal variation depends on your stage of life

Count a cycle from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Twenty-eight days is a familiar example, not a deadline everyone should meet. NHS information describes twenty-one to thirty-five days as common in adults, while age, circumstances and the person’s usual pattern affect interpretation.

Cycles can be less predictable in the years after periods begin and during the transition toward menopause. Breastfeeding and some contraceptive methods are other reasons for infrequent or absent bleeding. Those situations should not be treated as proof that every long gap is harmless.

A change outside your usual pattern does not automatically identify one of exactly eight diseases. The following possibilities are a guide for discussion, not a self-diagnosis checklist.

Stress can disturb the brain–ovary signals

The hypothalamus in the brain helps coordinate hormone signals that support ovulation. Stress can disrupt that signalling and can also change sleep, eating and daily routines. Illness or changes in weight may occur alongside it, making the pattern more complicated than one stressful day causing one missed period.

Relaxation techniques, a steadier routine and appropriate emotional support may help. However, stress should not be blamed before pregnancy and relevant medical causes have been considered.

More exercise is not a universal solution. Activity that supports wellbeing is different from adding demanding training when you are already exhausted or under-fuelled. Tell the clinician about the whole routine rather than trying to correct the cycle by exercising harder.

Low energy intake, eating disorders and heavy training

Ovulation may be disrupted when the body does not have enough available energy. This can occur with anorexia nervosa or bulimia, major weight loss, restrictive eating, or exercise demands that are not matched by food intake. It can also happen without a diagnosed eating disorder.

There is no reliable rule that exactly ten percent below an expected body weight is the point at which periods stop. Body size alone does not establish whether a person is adequately nourished. Someone training for a marathon, for example, may need assessment of energy intake, training and recovery rather than praise for losing their periods.

Treatment may include more adequate nutrition, reduced exercise and psychological or eating-disorder support. Prolonged disruption can affect bone health. Seek professional help rather than trying to manage an eating disorder or a long absence of periods alone.

Higher weight can be part of the picture, but is not a diagnosis

Higher body weight and substantial weight changes can be associated with altered ovulation and hormone patterns. That does not mean weight explains every late period in a larger person, or that an examination and other tests can be skipped.

If weight-related factors contribute, the clinician may discuss sustainable eating and activity changes alongside any underlying hormonal or metabolic condition. The plan should consider pregnancy intentions, medical history and the risk of restrictive or disordered eating.

A generic instruction to lose weight or start strenuous exercise may be inappropriate. Ask what the assessment found and what outcome a proposed change is intended to improve, rather than assuming a number on a scale provides the whole answer.

PCOS, now also called PMOS, can affect ovulation

The condition long known as polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, in current NHS guidance. You may encounter either name in health records. Irregular or absent ovulation, androgen-related symptoms and metabolic factors can all be relevant.

Androgens are hormones present in everyone; describing them only as male hormones can be misleading. Higher levels or effects may contribute to symptoms such as increased facial hair or acne. Insulin resistance may also be part of the condition.

The small follicles described in the older name are not ordinary ovarian cysts blocking menstrual blood. Diagnosis is based on the overall clinical picture. Treatment may address bleeding patterns, metabolic health, symptoms or fertility, depending on your priorities. A prescribed hormonal method may manage bleeding, but it is not the same as restoring spontaneous ovulation.

Starting or stopping contraception changes the interpretation

Hormonal contraception may make bleeding lighter, irregular or absent. Combined pills contain an oestrogen and a progestogen; other methods use a progestogen alone. It is incorrect to assume that every contraceptive pill has the same ingredients or effect on ovulation.

Bleeding can change after starting or stopping a method. Fertility generally returns promptly after stopping the combined pill, while an injection can have a longer-lasting effect. An implant and an injection are not interchangeable when discussing how long a change may last.

Do not wait six months automatically before asking about absent periods after stopping the pill. Consider test timing, your previous pattern and any symptoms. If pregnancy is not wanted, arrange contraception rather than relying on the absence of bleeding.

Chronic illness includes diabetes and coeliac disease

A significant chronic illness can affect menstrual function. Diabetes is one possible contributor, especially when health and glucose management are unsettled, but a missed period alone cannot show that diabetes is the cause. Review glucose care with the treating team rather than changing medicines to produce a period.

Coeliac disease can damage the small intestine and interfere with nutrient absorption. Delayed or missed periods can be among its effects, with or without prominent digestive symptoms. Persistent bowel problems, unexplained nutritional deficiencies or other relevant findings may prompt testing.

Do not diagnose coeliac disease from menstrual changes or start a gluten-free diet solely as a period remedy. If testing is being considered, discuss diet first because removing gluten can affect the results. Other illnesses and medicines may also need consideration.

Menopause symptoms before forty-five deserve attention

The usual menopause transition often occurs between forty-five and fifty-five, with changing cycle patterns before periods stop. Hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness or sleep changes can add useful context, but one late period does not establish menopause.

Changes before forty-five should be assessed; before forty, a clinician may investigate premature ovarian insufficiency. This is not simply a conclusion that every egg has disappeared, and appropriate blood tests and clinical history are needed.

Ovarian activity can sometimes occur intermittently in premature ovarian insufficiency. Pregnancy can therefore remain possible, although fertility is reduced. Discuss contraception or fertility support according to your plans, together with treatment for symptoms and longer-term health.

Both an overactive and an underactive thyroid can matter

Thyroid hormones influence many body functions, and either too much or too little thyroid activity can disturb ovulation and menstrual patterns. Fatigue, temperature sensitivity or weight changes may provide clues, but menstrual disruption can occur without an obvious thyroid symptom.

A clinician may check thyroid function as part of the assessment and interpret any abnormal result alongside other findings. Treatment of a thyroid disorder may help the cycle, but it does not guarantee that every menstrual change will resolve immediately.

Other hormone conditions, including raised prolactin, are also possible. Tell the clinician about medicines, headaches or unexpected milk discharge, without assuming that those symptoms establish one diagnosis.

Keep a record and arrange the right assessment

Record the start and end of bleeding, the usual cycle length, pregnancy-test dates, contraception and recent health changes. Include eating patterns, exercise, stress and any medicines or supplements. A short factual record is more helpful than guessing which hormone is responsible.

Seek assessment if you have missed three periods in a row without a known explanation, if your first period has not started by fifteen, or earlier for a substantial change or other symptoms. Formal specialist definitions vary with previous cycle regularity; they are not instructions to delay help when something is wrong.

Testing may include pregnancy testing, hormone blood tests or ultrasound, chosen according to the history. The aim is to address the cause and your health needs, not merely trigger a bleed with an unprescribed medicine.

Symptoms that should not wait for a routine review

When pregnancy is possible, one-sided lower abdominal pain, unusual bleeding or shoulder-tip pain needs prompt assessment, even without a positive test. Sudden severe pain, fainting, marked dizziness or collapse is an emergency.

Heavy bleeding with weakness, severe pain, fever or feeling very unwell also needs urgent care. Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down warrants prompt advice. A period lasting more than seven days should be discussed, but duration alone does not determine whether it is an emergency.

Any bleeding after established menopause should be checked, even if light or only once. In the usual setting, menopause is identified after twelve months without periods when hormonal contraception is not obscuring the pattern. Do not dismiss new bleeding as a normal restart.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A properly timed pregnancy test is an early step when pregnancy is possible.

Persistent absent periods deserve assessment of the cause, including nutrition, medicines and hormonal conditions.

How BeMama can help

Bring a simple cycle and symptom record to your appointment and explain whether your priority is contraception, conception, symptom relief or understanding the change.

When to seek help

Severe pelvic pain, faintness or heavy bleeding needs urgent care. Bleeding after menopause should be assessed even when light.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Twenty-eight days is not a required cycle length.
  • Stress, training and nutrition need context; exercise or weight loss is not the answer for everyone.
  • PCOS/PMOS is not an ordinary cyst blocking a period.
  • Contraceptive methods have different effects on bleeding and fertility return.
  • Thyroid disease, chronic illness and ovarian function may need investigation.

Frequently asked questions

When should I test if my cycle is unpredictable?

At least twenty-one days after the most recent unprotected sex, following the test instructions.

Can I trust a negative test taken before my period was due?

It may be too early. Repeat at the appropriate time and seek advice if the period remains absent.

Can stress be the reason?

Yes, but it should not be used to dismiss pregnancy or other relevant causes.

Do I need to be visibly underweight for low energy availability to matter?

No. Body size alone does not show whether food intake meets your needs.

Should I increase exercise to bring back my period?

Not automatically. If training exceeds available energy, reducing exercise and improving nutrition may be more appropriate.

Does PCOS mean cysts are preventing blood from leaving the uterus?

No. The condition involves ovulatory, hormonal and metabolic features, not a simple blockage by cysts.

Should I wait six months after stopping the pill?

There is no blanket waiting rule. Discuss persistent absence, symptoms and possible pregnancy with a clinician.

Can coeliac disease affect periods without obvious stomach problems?

It can have symptoms outside the gut. A clinician should decide whether testing is appropriate.

Does premature ovarian insufficiency mean pregnancy is impossible?

No. Ovarian activity can occur intermittently; discuss your pregnancy intentions and care needs.

When should an unexplained absence be checked?

Arrange assessment after three missed periods, or earlier for concerning symptoms or a major change; no first period by fifteen also needs review.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
